messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 22-year-old Latin American man who works as an HVAC technician and presented for intake following a workplace accident that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He had been performing routine maintenance on a rooftop unit at a commercial building when a colleague, working nearby on an adjacent platform, lost his footing on a surface Mateo had recently cleared of debris. Mateo had moved a safety cable to access a panel and had not yet re-secured it when his colleague fell, dropping nearly twelve feet onto a lower ledge. The man survived but sustained a severe spinal injury and has not returned to work. Mateo was the last person to handle that cable. He knows this with a certainty that has never loosened its grip on him.

In the weeks after the accident, Mateo found himself returning compulsively to every decision he had made that morning — the angle at which he had moved the cable, whether he had called out a warning, how many seconds had passed before he heard the impact. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt irrefutable, that he had failed to do what any competent person would have done, and that this failure revealed something permanent and damning about who he was. The person he saw in the mirror each morning felt unrecognisable — not the steady, capable young man who had taken pride in the trade, but someone whose hands could not be trusted and whose body had proven itself unreliable in the moment that mattered most. These appraisals drove him toward a set of strategies that seemed, at first, like reasonable self-management. He stopped attending the quarterly safety briefings at work, rerouted his morning commute to avoid the street where the building stood, and quietly marked the date of the accident on his calendar only to spend the entire week surrounding it in a state of preemptive withdrawal, calling in sick and barely leaving his apartment. Yet the more he contracted his world in this way, the more his sense of himself as damaged and culpable deepened — the avoidance itself became evidence of his guilt, proof that he could not face what he had done.

The memories did not stay contained. They forced their way into his mind without invitation — during a service call, while eating, in the middle of a conversation — and when they arrived they carried a sensory completeness that was almost unbearable. He could smell the rooftop: the hot tar, the metallic bite of the HVAC housing, something faintly chemical from the sealant he had been using. The memory had a quality he struggled to articulate, as though it had happened to someone else and he was watching footage of a stranger, and yet the smell and the sound were entirely his own. His conviction that he was unforgivable seemed to pull the memory forward more insistently, as though the mind were returning again and again to a wound it could not close.

The memories, in turn, had recoloured the world around him. On job sites now — crawl spaces, mechanical rooms, flat rooftops — Mateo's body responded before his thoughts could intervene: heart rate spiking, hands going cold, breath shortening into something close to panic. He had come to feel safe only in a small number of places: his apartment, his mother's kitchen, occasionally his truck. Unusual silence on a job site — the moment between shutting down a unit and the ambient noise returning — had become a specific source of dread, as though something catastrophic was always about to fill that quiet. This hypervigilant orientation to his environment kept him in a state of perpetual readiness that, in turn, made intrusive recall more likely; the body already braced, the memory needing little invitation.

The strategies he had built around all of this had cost him concretely. His supervisor had begun assigning him to solo residential calls rather than commercial sites, reading his reluctance to work at height as a performance concern. Mateo had not corrected this impression. He had stopped explaining himself to anyone.

What finally brought him in was a conversation with his mother, who told him quietly that she no longer recognised her son. He had heard something in that — an echo of his own worst fear — and made the call the following morning. What he most hoped for, he said at the end of the intake, was to be able to work again without his body betraying him. What he most feared was that the person he had been before the accident was simply gone.
